creator: drarielostad
caption:
A new chapter in melanoma treatment is emerging.

Recent Phase 3 results surrounding a personalized mRNA melanoma vaccine have generated significant attention—and for good reason. But what does a “melanoma vaccine” actually mean?

In this video, Dr. Ostad explains what this new research means, why it matters, and why knowing your skin remains as important as ever.

Unlike a traditional vaccine, this investigational therapy is not designed to prevent someone from developing melanoma. Instead, it
transcript: Hi, everyone. I wanted to just spend a couple of minutes about yesterday's results in the news, about how there is a melanoma vaccine that is now available. It's incredibly exciting, but I just wanted to spend a couple of minutes and break it down. This is not a melanoma vaccine that prevents melanoma, like a typical, let's say, flu vaccine or other vaccines that are given during childhood. So it's not that. It's not a vaccine that will prevent melanoma from ever forming in a patient. However, it is a vaccine that's used in advanced melanoma cases in cases where there is an increased risk of melanoma either recurring or spreading potentially later on to other organs or lymph nodes. So in the past, there were immunotherapy treatments such as Keytruda that basically have been shown to increase survival by reducing the chance of the cancer spreading or coming back. But now there is, in addition to immunotherapy, a melanoma vaccine by Moderna that basically is a personalized mRNA vaccine. And basically the way it works is that once someone has a melanoma that's high risk for coming back or spreading, it's that melanoma studied for specific gene mutations. And then a vaccine is actually developed to target that specific mutation in that patient's melanoma. So it's an exciting personalized vaccine that's developed for each patient depending on their mutation. And the combination of immunotherapy and that vaccine in phase three trials has been shown to actually reduce recurrence or spread by anywhere from 49 to 59%. The data still hasn't completely been published to truly see if actually prolonged survival. But it's incredibly promising that these are patients that will tend to have a disease-free survival for many more years. So it's really exciting news. Hopefully this will be approved in 2027. But I just wanted to tell you the good news. It's really mainly targeted towards patients who have advanced melanoma, basically where there's a higher risk of it spreading or coming back. It's not a vaccine that prevents melanoma. Thank you.

creator: drarielostad
caption:
There has been a growing trend, particularly among plastic surgeons, of criticizing dermal filler and pointing to overfilled faces as evidence that patients should abandon injectables in favor of surgery.

I understand where some of that criticism comes from.

For years, aesthetic medicine went through an era where nearly every sign of aging seemed to have the same answer: add more volume. Cheeks, temples, jawlines, lips—every hollow became something to fill.

But when filler is repeatedly added
transcript: Hi everyone. I want to talk to you about the issues with regards to fillers and why do so many plastic surgeons suddenly seem to hate filler. They're not completely wrong about the problem, but I think they're blaming the wrong thing. The problem isn't really the filler, it's how the filler has been used. For years, we saw an era of static medicine where almost every sign of aging was treated by adding more volume, bigger cheeks, sharper jaw lines, fuller lips, filling every hollow, but filler was never really designed to fix everything. If the real problem is significant skin laxity or tissue descent, adding more filler isn't necessarily going to help too much. So sometimes the right answer is really a laser skin tightening treatment. Sometimes it's truly a facelift surgery, but sometimes it's absolutely the filler is needed. So as both a dermatologist and a surgeon, I use all these modalities and I don't believe that filler or surgery should be competing with each other. Filler can be incredibly effective when small amounts are placed strategically to restore support, improve proportion, and really subtly improve the face. So the mistake is treating filler like a commodity, one syringe for your cheek, two for your jawline, and faces don't really come in syringes, and the treatment should really follow the anatomy, not the trend. And sometimes the best filler treatment I can give a patient is telling them they don't need filler at all, because the future of really natural-looking aesthetics isn't filler versus surgery, it's better judgment.

title: Dr. Ariel Ostad Explins His Approach to Neuromodualtors
caption:
Dr. Ariel Ostad explains how he assesses patients for neuromodulators, evaluating muscle activity, facial symmetry, and expression. His individualized approach guides dosing and placement to soften expression lines while preserving natural movement.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Visit our official website –
http://www.drarielostad.com/

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
transcript: When I assess a patient for neurotoxin treatment, I don't begin by looking at individual wrinkles. I begin by looking at the face as a whole. Every muscle has a function and many of these muscles work in opposition to one another. So before deciding where to treat, I want to understand how the patient's face moves naturally. Let's start with the upper face. Raise your eyebrows for me. So that's from movement of a muscle called the frontalis, which gives you the ability to raise your eyebrow. That's what over time leads to these horizontal lines across your forehead. This is an area where we want to under treat actually. Treatment should always take the patient's individual anatomy and movement into consideration. So now give me a big smile. I'm looking at how far those lines extend, how strong the contraction is, and whether the movement is symmetrical from one side to the other. Because as people smile, some wrinkles form here too, so it actually smooths that area as well. Now I'm going to look at the lower face. Here we're seeing the activity of the depressorangular aris, otherwise known as the DAO. This muscle pulls down the corners of the mouth. In appropriately selected patients, neurotoxin can be used off-label to reduce some of that downward muscular pull. Now, clench your teeth for me. Here I can feel the masseter muscle contracting. The masseter is a very powerful muscle involved in chewing. Neurotoxin treatment of the masseter is another off-label application and may be considered in certain patients depending on their anatomy and treatment goals. So now wrinkle your chin for me. Here we're looking at the mentalist muscle. When this muscle contracts strongly, some patients develop this dimpled or textured appearance across the chin. Neuromodulators can also be used off-label in this area to temporarily reduce that muscular activity and soften its appearance. What I want patients to understand is that neuromodulator treatment isn't simply about chasing individual lines. The forehead, the eyes, the brows, mouth, chin, and jaw all contribute to the way a face moves and expresses itself. So ultimately, I want my patients to still look like themselves. And the goal isn't to eliminate expression altogether, it's to use our understanding of facial anatomy, therefore maintain that natural movement and balance.

current.subject: how he assesses a face for neurotoxin
current.claim: He reads the whole face's muscle movement and symmetry before choosing where and how much neurotoxin to inject, under-treating the forehead.
current.speaker: doctor

transcript: If someone comes in and they think that their Botox is not working as well as it used to, these are four things that I think about. First, there could have been a potential discrepancy with that batch of Botox, the way that it was diluted or handled. We don't like neurotoxin, whether it's Botox, Dysport, Xiamin, Jeuveau. We don't want them to sit at room temperature for prolonged periods of time. It can affect the efficacy of the neurotoxin. Sometimes if the dilution is slightly off, that can affect the potency of the neurotoxin. There is the occasional bad batch where the potency is a little bit different. That's very uncommon. Second is that person maybe just needs more Botox. For those people whose muscles do get stronger, they sometimes do need a gradual increase in some of their Botox amounts. And then third, sort of related to what I just said, is that we are also actively aging. Wrinkles are also getting deeper. The rate at which the wrinkles are getting deeper could be faster than what Botox is able to do for your face. So there could be that. And then fourth, this is super, super rare, but you can become immune or develop what are called neutralizing antibodies against the neurotoxin itself. Like I said, rare. Under 1% of people get this. Overall, Botox or any of the neurotoxins are very helpful, very consistent. These situations can happen, but not so often.

current.subject: why botox stops working
current.claim: Botox seeming to stop working is usually handling/dilution, needing a higher dose or ongoing aging; true antibody resistance is under 1%.

So we have these blood vessels that dilate very easily and then they stay dilated. They stay essentially in a fight or flight mode. We also have these neurovascular signals which are over exaggerated. And then we have inflammatory pathways that do not completely shut off, even when the skin looks calm. So we have this cycle of dysregulation that stays active and over time it weakens the skin barrier. And so essentially the skin does become sensitive, but sensitivity does not come first. Sensitivity comes secondary to that dysregulation. So that's why treating Rosacea like super delicate skin that must avoid everything can actually keep you stuck in this cycle because essentially you are treating the symptom, you're not treating the driver of the actual problem. So while a lot of people use the word sensitive to describe Rosacea, it's actually poorly regulated and super over reactive. So remember this lady? Well, here she is again and she's been clear for over two years with zero problems with any flare ups. So long-term improvement is going to come from restoring the normal signaling within the skin and stabilizing the tissue. So sensitivity is what you see, it's what you feel, but what's actually happening is dysregulation. So if you can get the skin to regulate, you will get long-term results.

current.subject: rosacea is dysregulation not sensitivity
current.claim: Rosacea's root problem is vascular and inflammatory dysregulation, not sensitivity, so babying the skin keeps you stuck.
